headline: SW wind loads the Monomoy rips, bass pinned to the seams — bonito watch is on
subhead: Fluke steady on Horseshoe Shoal, stripers working the current edges at Great Point, and the first bonito scouts should be showing on the Shoals any day now.
body_markdown:
We've had a week of that classic mid-July SW breeze, ten to fifteen most afternoons, and it's done exactly what it always does out here — it stacks water against the ebb at Monomoy and turns a lazy tide into a genuine current edge you can fish. Last week's new moon pushed the tides up, and we're building back toward the first quarter around the 20th, which means the range is still healthy but not the washing-machine spring tide you get around the full or new. That's a good thing right now. Big spring tides blow the bait through the rips too fast for the bass to set up on it; this in-between range lets fish hold a lane and actually work it instead of getting flushed past. Surface water in the Sound has been sitting warm — the kind of warm where you can feel it through your waders at Bass River flats by mid-morning — while the water out over the Shoals stays noticeably cooler where the upwelling keeps grinding. That gradient is the whole story of this week's fishing.

Coming into this weekend, expect the SW flow to hold most days with a light backing to south late in the week as a weak front slides through the Gulf of Maine and grazes us without doing much. Tides will keep building toward the 20th, so look for the better current on the second half of the ebb at Monomoy and the first hour of the flood at Great Point — those are the windows where the seams are sharpest and the bait gets squeezed hardest.

Stripers have been the most consistent player. Monomoy Point and the rip off the south end of the island have been holding fish on the meat of the outgoing, especially where that SW wind piles against the current and turns a soft edge into a hard one you can actually see from the boat. I've had the best luck working white and chartreuse bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounces, bounced right along the seam where the color changes from sandy tan to that deeper green — cast up-current, let it sink on a controlled fall, and work it back with the current instead of against it. Fish have been mostly schoolies and mid-twenties, but there've been enough fish pushing 34 to 36 inches mixed in to keep everyone honest. Great Point has fished a similar pattern on the early flood — sand eels are thick along that rip line right now, and a Deadly Dick or a Hogy sand eel in olive over white, worked with a stop-and-go retrieve right in the white water, has been drawing hits from both bass and some quality bluefish in the 6 to 8 pound range. Those blues have been aggressive enough that wire or at least a heavy fluoro leader is worth the trouble — I lost two good bucktails to bite-offs last Tuesday alone.

Fluke have quietly been the most dependable box-filler out here. Horseshoe Shoal and the flats off Bass River have both been holding keeper fish in that 25 to 30 foot range on sandy-mud bottom, and honestly this has been one of the better fluke stretches we've had on the Shoals side in a couple seasons. Drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, has out-produced bare bucktails two or three to one when the drift is slow — and on these building tides the drift has mostly been manageable, not the screaming current you get on the springs. Keep the rod tip low and let the bait bump bottom; most of the bites out there have been subtle thumps, not the classic slam.

Here's the part everybody's been asking me about at the dock — bonito. Not yet. I know some guys are itching, and the water's certainly warm enough in the Sound proper, but I haven't had a confirmed bonito report off Nantucket Shoals yet this season, and albies at Great Point are still a good five or six weeks out on the calendar, historically. What I am seeing that gets my attention: bay anchovies are starting to show in the pockets along the south shore and around Tuckernuck, and that's usually the leading edge of the pattern that eventually pulls bonito up onto the Shoals in late July into early August. If that bait holds and the water out over the Shoals keeps its temperature — right now it's colder than the Sound itself, which is normal for this time of year — I'd expect the first bonito scout reports within two to three weeks, probably showing first on the eastern edge of the Shoals where the cooler, cleaner water meets bait pushed off the beach.

If I had one day this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Monomoy with bucktails, then run over to Great Point for the top of the flood and throw sand eel imitations through the rip while the light's still good. Fluke would be my backup plan if the wind lays down enough to sit comfortably on Horseshoe Shoal — that bite's been steady enough that it's hard to go wrong there even on a mediocre tide. Watch the SW wind through the weekend; if it holds in the fifteen-plus range for multiple days, the rips will keep loading up nicely, but if it swings hard south or picks up past twenty, I'd rather fish the lee side flats than fight standing water at Monomoy. Either way, keep an eye out for bait showing along the beaches — that's your first tell that the bonito switch is about to flip.
